The modulo \(13\) inverses of \(1,2,\dots,12\) are just the same set \(\{1,2,\dots,12\}\) in some order, since \(13\) is prime.

So the sum of the inverses modulo \(13\) is
\[
1+2+\cdots+12=\frac{12\cdot 13}{2}=78.
\]
Modulo \(13\),
\[
78 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}.
\]

message.content:
Since \(13\) is prime, every nonzero residue modulo \(13\) has a unique inverse. The first \(12\) positive integers are

\[
1,2,3,\dots,12,
\]

which are exactly the nonzero residues modulo \(13\). Taking inverses modulo \(13\) permutes this set, so the sum of the inverses is congruent to the sum of \(1,2,\dots,12\).

\[
1+2+\cdots+12=\frac{12\cdot 13}{2}=78
\]

Modulo \(13\),

\[
78 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}.
\]

The answer is 0.
